newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Gabon meeting seen crucial for Mobutu's next move.
newsitem.headline: Gabon meeting seen crucial for Mobutu's next move.

text.p: With time running out, Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko is expected to meet African leaders in Gabon on Wednesday where diplomats hope "he will do the right thing."

The "right thing" is to resign, turn over power to parliament which in turn could name someone who could negotiate a peaceful transfer of power, according to envoys and U.N. sources close to the manoeuvring.
In the best possible scenario, talks would then begin with rebel leader Laurent Kabila, whose forces in six months swept through most of Zaire and are nearing Kinshasa.

"He would be an important player but he should not take over entirely," said one U.N. source. "There is a political class, a civil society that has to agree. You can't just tell Mobuto to give Kabila power and he takes over."
He said that U.N. special envoy Mohammed Sahnoun, who helped set up the Libreville talks, believed there was "one week left" to negotiate a settlement.

So far Kabila has given few indications he agrees. And Mobutu, suffering from prostate cancer, has not decided to go into exile without setting conditions nearly impossible to fulfil. Some Zairean envoys believe he wants to die in Kinshasa, not in France where he receives medical care.

Rebel forces, led by Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo, have swept throught the country meeting little opposition from government soldiers who have not been paid for months. They are closing in on Kinsasha amid fears the unpaid soldiers may panic and loot the city.
The talks in Libreville on the endgame will be attended by leaders of Cameroon, the Central Africa Republic, Chad, Congo, Equatorial Guinea, with Gabonese President Omar Bongo conducting the meeting.
All are supporters of Mobutu in contrast to Zaire's neighbours in the east -- Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda as well as Angola to the southwest.
For the moment, however, no further face-to-face talks are being planned between Mobutu and Kabila after an abortive meeting on a South African ship over the weekend.

Meanwhile, France, where Mobutu has a residence, is being briefed on the latest developments by Sahnoun. At the same time South African officials are dealing with "allies of Kabila", the sources said.

Bill Richardson, the special envoy of President Bill Clinton, intends to fly to Paris Wednesday to speak to French officials, resentful of what they perceive as increasing U.S. influence in Central Africa, beginning with Washington's ties to the Tutsi leadership in Rwanda.
Rwanda helped create Kabila's alliance six months ago during an uprising of ethnic Tutsis in eastern Zaire.

Richardson, who is U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, has been shuttling throughout the continent in an effort to get a peaceful settlement out of Kabila, was in South Africa on Tuesday meeting with Vice President Thabo Mbeki.
"We want to make sure we're coordinating with the French during the endgame in Zaire," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told Reuters.
